fixes.explanation: Close, friend, because mountains in a courtroom sound like a case against the whole world. But the text says, "For the LORD has a case against His people, and He will argue it against Israel…" (Micah 6:2). The mountains are called to hear it. The case is against Israel.

That's right. Micah 6:2 says, "For the LORD has a case against His people, and He will argue it against Israel…" The nations aren't in the dock at all. The mountains just get the front-row seats, and nobody asked them to bring cookies.

Good guess, friend, but that isn't in these words. In this verse the LORD asks, "My people, what have I done to you?" and then says, "Testify against Me how I have wearied you!" (Micah 6:3). He opens the floor for them to speak against Him, and the text doesn't bring up anyone else they trust.

Those are real names with real stories, but they're not the ones in this verse. Micah 6:4 says, "I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam." Joshua and Caleb were two of the twelve spies sent into Canaan (Numbers 13:6, 8, 16), so you're in the right part of the Bible, friend. Just a different page.

Nice names, but this verse is about the Egypt story, and that's a different chapter of history. Micah 6:4 says, "I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam." Eli was a priest, Hannah was the woman who prayed for a son, and Samuel was the son she bore (1 Samuel 1:9, 20).

Yes! The first offering it wonders about is this: "Should I come to Him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves?" (Micah 6:6). It's the one asking who starts the shopping list, and it's about to get a lot bigger.

A big trip sounds like something a person would do to be serious about God. Verse 5 does mention a journey, from Shittim to Gilgal, but that's not what verse 8 says He requires. It says, "And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?" (Micah 6:8). Justice, mercy and a humble walk can start wherever you're standing.
